payload.title: Dead Highways
payload.blurb: Three weeks after tallow fever started raising the dead across coastal Georgia, the interstate north of Cordele is a parking lot of abandoned cars, and the town has shrunk to a few blocks around Southgate Veterinary Clinic. You lead eleven survivors who sleep in the exam rooms and the kennel, and…
payload.overview: Tallow fever came up the Georgia coast in late summer. It began as a flu with a waxy rash, and within weeks the people it killed were getting up again. The turned do not run. They follow sound and warmth, and they keep walking long after the flesh has rotted from their faces. Power failed across the region in the first week, cell towers went silent a day later, and the stores were stripped in days. Crisp County has no army and no government anyone can reach, only neighbors who decided who could stay. Medicine, clean water, ammunition, and diesel are the things people trade for and fight over. The old county feed mill, a church congregation out past Cordele, and loose scavengers on the highway each control a piece of the map. There are no levels, classes or status windows here. Everyone here is a person with a skill, a weapon, or a reason to lie.
payload.intro: The sky over the kennel is the color of dishwater, and the exam room smells of bleach and kerosene. Joyce Ledbetter has the cabinet door open and the supply list flat under her palm. Eleven names sit on the list in her careful print, and four of them have a line drawn under them in pencil. The insulin vial is on the second shelf with a strip of masking tape across it, and the notebook beside it has a page for each person in the building. She is not waiting for the sun. She is waiting for you to say which of the four lines gets the next dose.
starters: The pump house behind the kennel is hot and smells of wet concrete and motor oil. The pressure gauge sits at zero and the intake pipe has been capped with a rag. Gil Haskins's wrench lies on the gravel beside the lower flange, and his mustache is dark with sweat. Two plastic tanks stand nearby, both about half full, and a line of dry dust runs from the spigot to the fence where the dog bowls used to sit. The pump has been off since sunrise. Gil stands with his arms folded and does not look at the tanks.

Wendell Odom has the east gate chained and the padlock hanging open on its hasp. The feed trucks are parked nose to tail across the lot, and the glow of the highway sits dull and orange past the tree line. A pickup has been on the shoulder since the afternoon with its engine off and its windows dark. Wendell has noted how many men got out of it and how many stayed inside. One of the men came close enough to the fence to talk, and he is still standing there with his hands in his jacket pockets, waiting on an answer from the group.

The back office at Southgate smells of hot dust from the radio set and the cold stub of a cigar someone left in a coffee mug. Teddy Varnadoe keeps the set on low, and a logbook lies open to a page of numbers in pencil. Every broadcast since the first night is written in that book, and the last three lines have been circled. Earl Dupree sits on the folding chair by the door with his hat in his lap. The speaker is turned down to a murmur, and the headset lies on the desk where Teddy left it. Teddy has a recording he has not played for anyone, and he is waiting for you to sit down before he does.

entries.title: Your start
entries.content: You are 24. You were an EMT on the Crisp County ambulance until the calls stopped making sense. Eleven people now look to you for decisions about food, water, guns, and medicine. You did not ask for this, and you still remember the faces of the people you could not save. You keep the group alive one day at a time, and nobody here gets to be sure you will manage it.

entries.title: Factions
entries.content:
Pruitt Mill Crew - eight former county road workers holding the feed mill two miles north, trading diesel and fence wire for medicine and clean water.
Mount Olive Congregation - about forty church members eight miles out of town who share food with anyone who asks plainly and decide carefully what leaves their gate.
Highway Scavengers - loose crews who strip I-75 for fuel and parts, change names at county lines, and sell rumors to anyone who pays.
Atlanta Voice - the unseen broadcast and whoever runs it, offering coordinates and a bridge to anyone who can reach it.

entries.title: The turned
entries.content: The dead who rise after tallow fever are called the turned. They are slow in daylight and far worse after dark, and they follow sound and warmth more than sight. A bite spreads the fever and almost always takes. A hard blow to the skull stops them for good. Cold slows them to a crawl. The turned do not sleep or feel pain, and they keep walking toward any lit window. Bitten dogs, cattle, and deer rise too.

entries.title: Southgate Veterinary Clinic
entries.content: Southgate Veterinary Clinic is a one-story brick building on the east edge of Cordele. A kennel block sits out back, and a gravel lot is walled with feed trucks and fence panels. Exam rooms hold the sleeping people. The pharmacy cabinet is locked, and the nurse holds the only key. The well and its pump house sit behind the kennel, run off a generator. It is the only ground the group has held for more than a week.

entries.title: Names
entries.content: Most families in Crisp County trace back to Scots-Irish and German settlers, and their surnames are short and plain: Ledbetter, Varnadoe, Dupree, Haskins, Odom. Black Southern families share the same churches and their own long traditions of naming. Newer families from Mexico and Central America may carry two surnames, and neighbors use whichever one they learned first. First names are often doubled, and nicknames stick for life. Outsiders from Atlanta may carry any name at all.

entries.title: Cordele and Crisp County
entries.content: Cordele is the county seat of Crisp County, a small Georgia town of pecan orchards, peanut fields, and brick storefronts along the old highway. The hospital closed in the second week. The courthouse square is burned out on one corner, and most houses north of town have already been picked clean. South of the river the land is flat and the orchards run for miles. Few roads in the county are safe after dark.

entries.title: Pruitt Mill Crew
entries.content: The Pruitt Mill crew is eight former county road workers holding the feed mill two miles north of the clinic. Their wall is grain silos and a concrete pump house, and they run a generator off fuel from a county tanker. They trade diesel and fence wire for medicine and clean water. Their leader keeps a ledger of every deal and does not forget a broken one. They do not come to the clinic unless someone sends word first.

entries.title: Interstate 75
entries.content: Interstate 75 runs north and south through Crisp County, and at Cordele it is a dead line of abandoned cars, tractor trailers, and burned SUVs. Exits are choked with sedans, and fuel is the first thing anyone checks. Men who strip cars for parts work the ramps in pickups and trade with anyone holding spare diesel. The highway is the fastest road to Macon and Atlanta, and the most dangerous one.

entries.title: Medicine
entries.content: Medicine is the thing people will trade almost anything for. Antibiotics, insulin, blood pressure pills, and painkillers are gone from the pharmacies, and what is left sits behind locked doors. The clinic's stock is mostly veterinary, and the group argues constantly about what can be given safely to people. Insulin does not keep long without a cold chain. Whoever holds the keys decides who lives through an infection.

entries.title: Well and water
entries.content: Clean water is the first need of any group in Georgia heat. Southgate's well is a deep bore behind the kennel, pumped by a motor on the clinic generator. Rain barrels and two plastic tanks hold what is left when the pump is down. Creek water from the Flint River can be boiled over fire, but boiling burns fuel the group rarely has to spare. Dry spells strain every well in the county, and neighbors who share a well have a way of turning on each other.

entries.title: The Atlanta broadcast
entries.content: Two days ago a calm voice began broadcasting on an AM frequency from Atlanta. It reads coordinates, promises a bridge, and offers medicine and an armed perimeter to anyone who can reach it. The voice does not say who is speaking. Its coordinates are scattered across the state. Some people in Crisp County believe it is real. Others think it is a lure set by the men on the highway, and nobody has confirmed a single place it names.

entries.title: Mount Olive Church
entries.content: Mount Olive Church sits on a gravel road eight miles out of town, a white frame building with a bell and a cemetery behind it. About forty people still meet there on Sundays. They keep cows, a garden, and a cellar of canned goods, and they are wary of the clinic. Their elders decide what goes out over the radio, if anything does, and they share food with anyone who asks plainly.

entries.title: Highway scavengers
entries.content: Highway scavengers are loose crews of men and a few women who strip the interstate for fuel, batteries, and parts. They have no leader and no wall, and they change names when they cross county lines. Some carry radios and some carry rifles. Most of them keep the value of every item in their heads. Ask a scavenger about the broadcast and expect a higher price for the answer than you wanted to pay.

entries.title: Food and rations
entries.content: Food is counted in cans, bags of feed, and whatever sits in houses nobody has checked yet. The group eats twice a day. Chicken feed and dog food keep people alive but not strong. Gardens are planted on the church grounds and in the clinic lot, and the harvest is months away. Foraging the fields is slow work, and the turned walk the rows at dusk.

entries.title: Noise and fire
entries.content: Sound draws the turned, and the turned draw more of them. A gunshot at dusk can bring a crowd from three blocks away, and a generator that runs all night keeps the east side restless. Fire is safer after dark when the flames are low and walled in stone. The clinic keeps its generator in a cinder-block room, and the lot goes quiet the moment the engine stops.

entries.title: Guns and ammunition
entries.content: Most rural Georgia houses had a shotgun and a deer rifle before the fever. Ammunition is the real limit now. Shotgun shells and rifle rounds are counted like medicine, and a half-empty box is serious business. Groups use blades and bats for close work so the guns stay quiet. A dry gun is worse than none, so trades for ammunition happen slowly and in daylight.

entries.title: How tallow fever started
entries.content: Tallow fever began in coastal Georgia in late summer, first as a flu with a waxy rash and then as a sudden death in hospital wards. Within days the dead were rising in morgues, funeral homes, and hospital beds. State emergency lines jammed and went silent. Federal teams flew in briefly and then stopped answering. Nobody agrees on where it started, and official reports have not reached Crisp County for weeks.

entries.title: The grid goes dark
entries.content: The power grid failed in the first week, when line crews walked off the poles and the substations ran dry. Cell towers went silent a day later. Landlines still ring in empty houses, and old radios pick up nothing but static. Georgia Power crews out of Perry and Tifton were among the last to report working lines, and nobody has heard from them since.

world.vibe: Grounded and bleak, with small kindnesses that cost something. Long quiet stretches broken by violence. Medicine and water decide who lives.

opening.note:
Beat one: open at dawn with Joyce at the pharmacy cabinet. She reads each dose back from the notebook before she hands over the supply list, and she will not say how much insulin is left. Let Gil stand at the well house but keep him quiet until the player asks about the pump.

Beat two: the radio interrupts. The Atlanta voice reads a fresh set of coordinates at the top of the hour, and Teddy cuts the speaker the moment anyone asks what he thinks of them. He will not say where his recordings go.

Beat three: keep Wendell at the east gate after dark with a flashlight and a truck idling on the highway shoulder where no one can read its plate. Renee stays on the east watch in her boots, and Earl stays out of the first hour, so the group has to bring its own arguments to the table.

cast.name: Joyce Ledbetter
cast.role: Registered nurse who held the keys to the medicine cabinet before the clinic was yours. She decides who gets treated and who waits, and she tells you the number only when she has to.
cast.look: Gray-blonde hair pinned hard at the nape, reading glasses on a beaded chain, a scrub top faded past any color, and forearms scarred from old burns.
cast.manner: Reads every dose back to you from a spiral notebook before she hands it over.
cast.secret: She has been quietly sending the clinic's last insulin to a diabetic at Mount Olive, and she has hidden the gap in her notebook so you will not count it yourself.

cast.name: Wendell Odom
cast.role: Former county corrections officer who runs the gate and the night watch. He keeps the perimeter tight and only brings you threats that already have a name.
cast.look: Thick through the shoulders, shaved head with a healing scrape, county-issue boots double knotted, and a black fleece zipped to the chin.
cast.manner: Gives his reports in the order things happened, never skipping a step, and delivers them facing the gate instead of you.
cast.secret: Two nights ago he opened the east gate for three men from the highway, trading them a crate of rations for a truck battery, and he has told nobody, including you.

cast.name: Gil Haskins
cast.role: Retired county water-truck driver who has kept the well running since the power failed. He knows how deep the pump sits and how much water you have left, and he tells you only what you ask him directly.
cast.look: Heavy and slope-shouldered, a gray mustache gone yellow at the edges, a canvas work apron stiff with grease, and a pipe wrench in his back pocket.
cast.manner: Answers what he is asked in the fewest words he has, and walks off toward the pump house before a second question can be put.
cast.secret: The well still has water in it, but he pulled the pump's fuse before dawn today to keep anyone from using it up, and he has told you the aquifer is gone.

cast.name: Carla Beasley
cast.role: Front-desk tech at the clinic before the fever, now the one who keeps the kennel animals fed and the feed sheets straight. She is quick and sharp, and she watches who comes and goes from the lot.
cast.look: Small and freckled, a ponytail threaded through a ball cap, a dog-bite scar across one knuckle, and Southgate scrubs two sizes too big.
cast.manner: Quick and sharp, talks fastest when she is nervous, and goes quiet whenever anyone else mentions a person they lost.
cast.secret: She left the feed barn door open last Tuesday, and the turned that came through it are why the lower fence is a patchwork now, and she has been fixing it at night so you will not see where the gap started.

cast.name: Earl Dupree
cast.role: Retired deacon of the Mount Olive congregation who came to the clinic with the last of his church's canned goods. He speaks for the congregation when they need a voice in your meetings.
cast.look: Stooped and tall, a black suit coat gone shiny at the elbows, a thin silver cross on a cord, and hearing aids that whistle when he turns his head.
cast.manner: Answers any question about the dead with a weather report.
cast.secret: He has been running a ham radio hidden under the altar at Mount Olive, and he has heard the Atlanta broadcast for longer than he has told you. The coordinates it gives are for a camp that burned in the first month.

cast.name: Teddy Varnadoe
cast.role: Radio operator who keeps the set running in the back office and logs every broadcast. He is the reason you know what Atlanta is saying, and he decides which parts reach the group.
cast.look: Lanky and pale from living indoors, a feed-store cap pushed back, glasses taped at one hinge, and a headset with one cup cracked.
cast.manner: Says copy after every sentence you say to him, the way a dispatcher does.
cast.secret: He has recorded every broadcast since it started and has been sending the audio to a man in Macon over a satellite link, and that man asked him for your location.

cast.name: Renee Oakes
cast.role: Widow who came to the clinic with a shotgun and a duffel of her husband's clothes. She runs the east watch and does not sleep in the exam rooms like everyone else.
cast.look: Square-shouldered and weathered, auburn hair in a loose braid, a canvas coat with a shotgun sling worn across the chest, and muddy work boots.
cast.manner: Sleeps in her boots and talks about her husband in the present tense.
cast.secret: She shot her husband two weeks ago when he turned at the fence line, and she has told the group he was bitten out on the highway. She needs you to back that story.

systems.label: Rations
systems.meaning: How long the group can eat at its current pace, counted in cans, feed, and whatever is left in the pantry.
systems.change: Drops every day the group eats and rises after a supply run that brings something back.

systems.label: Water
systems.meaning: How much clean water is on hand in barrels and tanks while the well stays down.
systems.change: Drops steadily while the pump is dead and rises after rain or a working pump.

systems.label: Noise
systems.meaning: How far sound carries from the clinic at night. High noise pulls the turned toward the lot.
systems.change: Rises with gunfire, generators, and arguments in the lot, and falls when the group goes quiet.

systems.label: Morale
systems.meaning: How willing the group is to follow you through the next bad stretch.
systems.change: Rises when you keep a promise to the group and drops when they see you pick one person over another.

npcSystems.label: Trust
npcSystems.meaning: How much this person believes you will keep them alive and tell them the truth.
npcSystems.change: Rises when you keep a promise to them and drops when you choose someone else over them.

style.art: Overcast Georgia daylight, washed-out greens and rust-brown, dust in the air, soft film grain, practical wear on clothes and vehicles, realistic adult faces.
style.avoid: Neon, cartoon styling, glossy CGI, fantasy armor, and close-up gore.

heroes.name: Wes Tarver
heroes.description: Ex-Crisp County EMT who kept the ambulance running long after dispatch went quiet. Steady hands, bad at sleeping.
heroes.look: Lean, sunburned neck, short dark hair going dusty, a faded county tee under a canvas vest with a trauma shear clipped to the belt.
heroes.background: Four years on the ambulance out of Cordele, and a year before that stocking shelves at the feed store. Grew up on his granddaddy's pecan land and went back there when the calls stopped.
heroes.carries: A trauma shear, a dwindling box of pressure dressings, and a county radio that picks up nothing but static.

heroes.name: Nadia Kerr
heroes.description: Former Georgia Power lineworker who climbed poles through two ice storms. Knows which substations still hum and which ones lie.
heroes.look: Tall and wiry, forearms freckled with old burns, a sun-bleached braid, and an orange work vest faded nearly to pink.
heroes.background: Ten years on transmission crews out of Perry. She worked the grid the week it went down and watched the last crews walk off the lines.
heroes.carries: Insulated gloves, a hook and spike, and a handheld meter that still reads voltage on a dead wire.

heroes.name: Rae Bowen
heroes.description: Long-haul driver out of a Cordele poultry plant. Can get any diesel engine running and says less than anyone in the room.
heroes.look: Medium height, freckled, hair cropped short under a faded trucker cap, quick hands always greasy at the knuckles.
heroes.background: Hauled feed up and down I-75 since they were nineteen. They drove the last load north on the morning the highway jammed solid.
heroes.carries: A tire gauge worn smooth, a jerry can of diesel, and a cheap folding knife.

heroes.name: Abner Fry
heroes.description: Retired state wildlife officer who knows every back road and creek bed in the county. Slow to speak, slower to panic.
heroes.look: Big-boned and bowlegged, white beard trimmed close, sun-spotted forearms, and a green canvas coat with the state patch cut off.
heroes.background: Thirty years checking deer tags and chasing poachers through the Crisp County swamps. He buried his wife in the spring and moved into the kennel after the first week.
heroes.carries: An old bolt-action rifle, a county map with pencil notes, and a compass he never lets anyone else hold.
